title: Count Inversions
directAnswer: An inversion is a pair (i, j) with i < j but nums[i] > nums[j]. Counting them brute-force is O(n²). The interview answer is a modified merge sort: during the merge, when you pull an element from the right half before the left, every remaining element in the left half forms an inversion — add (mid − i + 1) at once, giving O(n log n).

remember.pattern: Modified merge sort — count cross-half inversions during the merge step
rules: Count inversions during the **merge**, the moment a right element is picked before left elements remain: add `(mid − i + 1)` — *all* leftover left elements at once, not one.
Use `<=` (not `<`) when comparing left vs right so **equal** elements aren't miscounted as inversions — equal pairs are not inversions.
The inversion count can be as large as `n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹` for `n = 10⁵` — use a 64-bit `long`, not `int`.
Total inversions = (inversions in left half) + (inversions in right half) + (cross-half inversions). Don't forget to sum the recursive returns.
The array gets sorted as a side effect; if the caller needs the original order, sort a copy.
whenToUse: Counting how 'out of order' an array is (number of swaps a bubble sort would do)
Measuring rank correlation / similarity between two orderings
Any 'count pairs where i < j and some order condition holds' over a large array
When an O(n²) pair scan is too slow and the condition is comparison-based
antiSignals: n is tiny → the brute force double loop is simpler and fine
You only need to know if *any* inversion exists → just check if the array is sorted in O(n)
Values are bounded small integers → a Binary Indexed Tree (BIT) over values is an alternative O(n log V)
remember.takeaway: Inversion counting is the canonical 'piggyback a count onto merge sort' problem. The single insight — when a right element jumps ahead of k remaining left elements, that's k inversions at once — is what turns O(n²) into O(n log n).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you connect 'count out-of-order pairs' to merge sort, and whether you get the cross-count right: adding all remaining left elements in one shot rather than incrementing by one.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting one inversion per right-element pick instead of (mid − i + 1), using `<` so equal elements get miscounted, or overflowing a 32-bit counter.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the three-part recurrence (left + right + cross), explain why the left half being sorted lets you batch-count, and note the long overflow up front.

problemStatement:
Given an array `nums`, count the number of **inversions** — pairs of indices `(i, j)` such that `i < j` and `nums[i] > nums[j]`.

Inversions measure how far the array is from sorted: a sorted array has `0`, a reverse-sorted array has the maximum `n(n−1)/2`.
constraints: The answer can reach ~5 × 10⁹ — return a 64-bit integer
understanding: Count pairs that are out of order. The brute force checks every pair; the efficient solution observes that merge sort already compares elements across the two halves, so we can tally cross-half inversions for free during the merge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are equal elements an inversion?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — an inversion requires strictly nums[i] > nums[j]. I'll use <= when comparing left to right so equals aren't counted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the count get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to n(n−1)/2, about 5 billion for n = 10⁵, so I return a long to avoid 32-bit overflow.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I modify (sort) the input array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Merge sort reorders it as a side effect. If you need the original preserved, I'll work on a copy.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Any bound on the values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If values were small bounded integers, a Binary Indexed Tree is an alternative; otherwise merge sort is the general O(n log n) answer.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Pair (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor correctness and define an inversion precisely, then upgrade for the time limit.
hints: An inversion is literally a pair (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] > nums[j]. What's the most direct way to count such pairs?
Two nested loops: outer i, inner j > i. Increment a counter whenever nums[i] > nums[j].
This is correct but O(n²). For n = 10⁵ that's 10¹⁰ comparisons — far too slow. What sorting algorithm naturally compares cross-pairs?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every ordered pair (i, j) with i < j is examined once: n(n−1)/2 comparisons → O(n²). Only a counter is stored.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the definition straight into code: for every `i`, scan every later `j` and increment a counter when `nums[i] > nums[j]`.

**Why it's the right way to understand the problem.** Before optimizing, make the definition concrete — an inversion is an out-of-order pair, and the double loop counts exactly those. Running it on `[2, 4, 1, 3, 5]` and watching it find `(2,1)`, `(4,1)`, `(4,3)` confirms your mental model and gives you a reference oracle to test the fast version against.

**Why `j` starts at `i + 1`.** Inversions are defined on `i < j`, so the inner loop begins just past `i`. This counts each unordered pair exactly once and never compares an element with itself.

**Why it doesn't survive the constraints.** At `n = 10⁵` the loop does ~`5 × 10⁹` comparisons — seconds to minutes, a guaranteed time-limit exceeded. The cost is fundamentally quadratic because it inspects pairs independently, learning nothing reusable. The fix is to count pairs in *bulk*, which is exactly what a merge does.
approaches.insight: The double loop is the definition made literal — perfect for correctness, useless for scale. Use it as the oracle you validate the merge-sort solution against.

approaches.name: Modified Merge Sort (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'count cross-half inversions for free during merge sort's merge step'.
hints: Split the array in half, recursively count inversions in each half. What kind of inversions are left to count after that?
Cross-half inversions: i in the left half, j in the right half. If both halves are sorted, can you count these efficiently while merging them?
During merge, when right[j] < left[i], element right[j] is smaller than left[i] AND every left element after i (they're sorted). So add (number of remaining left elements) all at once.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Merge sort's recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to O(n log n). The inversion counting adds only O(1) work per merge comparison, so it doesn't change the bound. The temporary merge buffer needs O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Run a standard merge sort, but during each merge tally the inversions that cross the two halves. The total is `inversions(left) + inversions(right) + cross-half inversions`.

**Why splitting captures every inversion exactly once.** Any inversion `(i, j)` has both indices in the left half, both in the right half, or one in each. The recursive calls handle the first two cases; the merge handles the third. Because the three categories are disjoint and exhaustive, summing them counts each inversion once — no double counting, no misses. This is the divide-and-conquer skeleton.

**The key insight — batch counting during merge.** When merging two *sorted* halves, you compare `left[i]` and `right[j]`. If `right[j] < left[i]`, then `right[j]` is smaller than `left[i]` — but since the left half is sorted ascending, `right[j]` is also smaller than `left[i+1], left[i+2], …` all the way to `mid`. So this single right element forms an inversion with *every* remaining left element. Instead of counting them one by one, add `(mid − i + 1)` in one stroke. That batching is precisely what removes the quadratic factor.

**Why `<=` and not `<` in the comparison.** When `left[i] == right[j]`, that pair is *not* an inversion (it needs strict greater-than). Taking the left element first on ties (`left[i] <= right[j]` → take left) avoids counting equal elements as inversions and also keeps the sort stable. Flip it to `<` and you over-count every duplicate that straddles the split.

**Why a long, and why O(n) space.** The maximum inversion count is `n(n−1)/2`, about `5 × 10⁹` for `n = 10⁵` — past the 32-bit range, so the accumulator must be `long`. The merge needs a temporary buffer of size O(n); that's the space cost, not the recursion stack (which is O(log n)).

**Why this generalizes.** The same 'count something during the merge' template solves 'count smaller elements to the right', 'reverse pairs' (`nums[i] > 2·nums[j]`), and 'range sum count'. Recognizing inversions as the prototypical instance is the transferable skill.
approaches.insight: Because the left half is sorted, one right element that jumps ahead is simultaneously smaller than *all* remaining left elements — so you count k inversions in O(1) instead of k steps. That batch count is the entire reason the algorithm is O(n log n).

dryRun.intro: Left = [2,4], Right = [1,3]. When a right element is taken before left elements remain, add the count of remaining left elements.

code.python:
def count_inversions(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
    def sort_count(arr: list[int]) -> tuple[list[int], int]:
        if len(arr) <= 1:
            return arr, 0
        mid = len(arr) // 2
        left, a = sort_count(arr[:mid])
        right, b = sort_count(arr[mid:])
        merged, cross = [], 0
        i = j = 0
        while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
            if left[i] <= right[j]:       # <= keeps equals out of the count
                merged.append(left[i]); i += 1
            else:
                merged.append(right[j]); j += 1
                cross += len(left) - i     # all remaining left elements > right[j]
        merged.extend(left[i:])
        merged.extend(right[j:])
        return merged, a + b + cross
    return sort_count(nums)[1]

pitfalls: Incrementing count by 1 instead of (mid − i + 1) — silently undercounts.
Using < instead of <=, miscounting equal straddling elements.
Storing the count in an int — overflows near 5 × 10⁹.
Forgetting to add the two recursive returns to the cross count.

commonMistakes: Counting one inversion per right-element pick instead of all remaining left elements.
Using < rather than <= so equal elements are miscounted.
Overflowing a 32-bit counter; the answer can reach ~5 × 10⁹.
Forgetting to sum the inversions returned by the two recursive halves.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Incrementing by one instead of batching
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When right[j] is taken, it inverts with EVERY remaining left element, not just left[i]. Adding 1 undercounts.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict < miscounts equals
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With <, when left[i] == right[j] you take the right element and count it as an inversion — but equal pairs are not inversions.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on the count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Maximum inversions n(n−1)/2 is ~5 billion for n = 10⁵, beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE. Accumulate in a long.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int count = 0;   // overflows for large reverse-sorted input

patternNote: Counting work piggybacked onto merge sort's divide-and-conquer. The reusable template: split, recurse, then count cross-boundary pairs during the merge using the sortedness of each half to batch the count. It also solves count-smaller-to-the-right and reverse-pairs.
